chapters.title: Section 1
paragraphs: Some things are within our control, others are not. Within our control are our opinions, impulses, desires, and aversions — in short, whatever is our own doing. Outside our control are our body, reputation, possessions, and positions of power — in short, whatever is not our own doing. What is within our control is by nature free, unhindered, unobstructed. What is outside our control is weak, dependent, subject to obstruction — it belongs to others. Remember: if you mistake what belongs to others for your own, you will be frustrated, you will grieve, you will be in turmoil, blaming gods and men alike. But if you take as your own only what truly is your own, and recognise that what belongs to others belongs to others, no one will ever compel you or obstruct you. You will blame no one, accuse no one, do nothing against your will. You will have no enemies, and nothing can harm you.

If you aim at such great things, remember you must not pursue them halfheartedly. Some things must be given up entirely, others set aside for now. But if you want both — inner freedom and worldly power and wealth — you may well get neither, because the pursuit of one undermines the other. You will certainly fail to secure the things through which alone happiness and freedom are possible. Practise saying to every difficult impression: "You are an impression, not the reality." Then test it above all by this rule: does it concern what is within my control, or what is not? If not, train yourself to say: "This is nothing to me."

chapters.title: Section 2
paragraphs: Desire carries within it the expectation of getting what you desire; aversion carries the expectation of avoiding what you turn from. Whoever fails to get what they desire is unfortunate; whoever falls into what they are trying to avoid is unhappy. So: if you try to avoid only what is unnatural among the things within your control, you will never encounter what you want to avoid. But if you try to avoid sickness, death, or poverty, you will be unhappy. Remove aversion from everything outside your control and redirect it toward what is genuinely harmful within your control. For now, set aside desire entirely. If you desire anything outside your control, you must meet with disappointment. The things worth desiring within your control are not yet before you. Use only gentle impulse toward and away from things, held loosely and tentatively.

chapters.title: Section 3
paragraphs: Whenever something pleases you, or meets a need, or that you love, remind yourself of its nature. Start with small things. If you love a clay cup, say to yourself: it is a clay cup that I love. When it breaks, you will not be disturbed. If you kiss your child or your wife, say: it is a human being I am kissing. When they die, you will not be disturbed.

chapters.title: Section 4
paragraphs: Before taking on any activity, picture what it involves. If you are going to the baths, picture what happens there — people splashing, jostling, arguing, stealing. Then you will go more safely if you say to yourself: I want to bathe, and I want to keep my will in accordance with nature. Do this with every activity. That way, if something gets in the way of your bathing, you can say: that was not all I intended — I also intended to keep my will in accordance with nature. And I will not do that by getting upset over what happens.

chapters.title: Section 5
paragraphs: People are not disturbed by events but by their opinions about events. Death, for instance, is nothing terrible — if it were, it would have seemed terrible to Socrates. What is terrible is the opinion that death is terrible. So whenever we are frustrated, troubled, or distressed, let us never blame others, but ourselves — meaning our own opinions. It is the sign of an untrained person to blame others for their troubles; of one beginning to learn, to blame themselves; of one whose learning is complete, to blame neither others nor themselves.

chapters.title: Section 6
paragraphs: Do not take pride in advantages that belong to someone else. If a horse could say proudly "I am beautiful," that would be tolerable. But when you say proudly "I have a beautiful horse," you should know that you are taking pride in something that belongs to the horse. What is actually yours? The use of your impressions. When you use your impressions in accordance with nature, then be proud — for then you are proud of something genuinely good, and genuinely yours.

chapters.title: Section 7
paragraphs: On a sea voyage, when the ship puts into port and you go ashore to fetch water, you might pick up a shellfish or a plant along the way — but keep your eyes on the ship. When the captain calls, leave everything and run back. That is how it is in life too. If instead of a shellfish you are given a wife and child, there is nothing wrong with that. But when the captain calls, leave even them without hesitation. And if you are old, don't wander far from the ship in the first place, lest you be left behind when the call comes.

chapters.title: Section 8
paragraphs: Don't seek for things to happen the way you want them to. Wish instead that what happens is exactly as it is, and you will find life flows with tranquility.

chapters.title: Section 9
paragraphs: Illness is an obstacle to the body, but not to the will, unless the will consents to it. Lameness is an obstacle to the leg, but not to the will. Apply this reflection to everything that happens to you: you will find it is an obstacle to something, but not to you.

chapters.title: Section 10
paragraphs: When any event befalls you, turn to yourself and ask what capacity you have to meet it. If you see someone attractive, the resource available to you is self-restraint. If you face hardship, it is endurance. If you are insulted, it is patience. Once you have formed this habit, events will not sweep you away.

chapters.title: Section 11
paragraphs: Never say about anything "I have lost it," but say "I have returned it." Is your child dead? They have been returned. Is your wife dead? She has been returned. Has your property been taken? That too has been returned. "But the one who took it is a bad person." What does it matter to you who the giver used to reclaim it? While you have it, treat it as a traveller treats an inn — care for it, but as something that belongs to another.

chapters.title: Section 12
paragraphs: If you are working to improve yourself, let go of thoughts like: "If I neglect my business I will have nothing to live on," or "If I don't discipline my servant he will become lazy." It is better to die of hunger free from grief and fear than to live in abundance troubled and anxious. And it is better for your servant to be lazy than for you to be miserable. Begin with small things. Oil spilled, wine stolen — say to yourself: this is the price of peace of mind; this is the price of tranquility. Nothing comes for free. When you call your servant, bear in mind that he may not hear, or hearing, may not do what you ask. He does not have the power to disturb you — but you have the power not to be disturbed.

chapters.title: Section 13
paragraphs: If you want to improve, be willing to be thought foolish and ignorant about external matters. Wish to appear to know nothing. And if you start to seem important in anyone's eyes, distrust yourself. Because it is not easy to both keep your will aligned with nature and pursue external things — whoever is careful about one will necessarily neglect the other.

chapters.title: Section 14
paragraphs: To wish your children, wife, and friends to live forever is foolish — you are wishing for things outside your control to be in your control, for what belongs to others to be yours. Equally, if you wish your servant to make no mistakes, you are wishing that what is bad were not bad. But if you want to succeed in your desires, that is something you can actually do. Practise what is in your power. The master of any person is whoever controls what that person wants or doesn't want — whoever can grant it or withhold it. Anyone who wants to be free must want nothing and avoid nothing that lies in another's power. Otherwise they are a slave.

chapters.title: Section 15
paragraphs: At a banquet, remember to behave like a proper guest. When a dish is passed to you, reach out and take your portion gracefully. When it passes by, don't hold it back. When it hasn't reached you yet, don't reach forward — wait until it comes to you. Do this with children, with a spouse, with public office, with wealth, and you will prove a worthy guest at the gods' own table. But if you don't even take what is offered, if you actually refuse it — then you will share not just the gods' banquet but their power. This is how Diogenes and Heraclitus and those like them earned the name divine.

chapters.title: Section 16
paragraphs: When you see someone weeping in grief — because a child has gone away, or died, or because they have lost property — be careful not to be carried away by the appearance that they are suffering from external events. Draw a distinction in your own mind and be ready to say: what distresses this person is not what has happened — the same thing would not distress someone else — but their opinion about what has happened. In your words, by all means sympathise with them and even share their grief if the moment calls for it. But do not grieve inside as well.

chapters.title: Section 17
paragraphs: Remember that you are an actor in a play whose length is determined by the author. If he wants it short, it is short; if long, long. If he wants you to play a poor man, play that role naturally; if a cripple, a magistrate, an ordinary person — do the same. Your duty is to act well the part you have been given. But choosing the part belongs to someone else.

chapters.title: Section 18
paragraphs: When a raven croaks ominously, don't be carried away by it. Immediately draw a distinction: none of this concerns me — it concerns my body, my property, my reputation, my children, my wife. But for me everything is auspicious, because whatever happens, it is in my power to benefit from it.

chapters.title: Section 19
paragraphs: You can be undefeatable if you never enter a contest where victory is not within your power. When you see someone honored, powerful, or highly regarded, be careful not to assume they are happy — don't be swept away by appearances. If what is good lies within our power, there is no place for envy or jealousy. You will not wish to be a general, a senator, a consul — you will wish to be free. And there is only one road to freedom: not caring about things outside your power.

chapters.title: Section 20
paragraphs: Remember that it is not the person who insults or strikes you who humiliates you, but your own opinion about what they have done. When someone angers you, know that it is your own judgment that has angered you. Most importantly: try not to be swept away in the moment. If you gain even a little time and pause, you will find it far easier to master yourself.

chapters.title: Section 21
paragraphs: Keep death before your eyes every day, and exile, and everything else that seems dreadful — above all, death. Then you will never think small thoughts, and you will never want for more than you need.

chapters.title: Section 22
paragraphs: If you commit yourself to philosophy, be prepared from the start to be laughed at, to have people sneer and say: "Look, a philosopher has appeared among us — where did he get that superior look?" Don't look superior. Hold fast to what seems best to you, as if assigned to that post by God. If you stand firm in your principles, those who ridiculed you will come to admire you. But if you are talked out of your purpose, you will earn double ridicule.

chapters.title: Section 23
paragraphs: If you ever find yourself turning toward external things in order to please someone, know that you have lost your purpose. Be content to be a philosopher in everything. And if you want to seem like one to others, first seem like one to yourself — that is all you need.

chapters.title: Section 24
paragraphs: Don't let thoughts like these trouble you: "I will go unrecognised and be nobody." If dishonor were actually evil, you could not be brought into evil by someone else's actions, any more than you can be brought into anything shameful. Is it really your job to get public office or to be invited to dinner parties? Not at all. How is missing those things any kind of dishonor? And how can you be "nobody" when you should only be somebody in the things that lie within your power — and in those things you can be a person of the greatest worth? "But my friends will go without help!" What do you mean? They won't receive money from you, and you won't make them citizens. Who told you that these are among the things in your power and not in someone else's? And who can give what they don't have? "Then earn money," your friends say, "so we can have something too." If I can earn money and at the same time remain honest and honorable and high-minded, show me the way and I will earn it. But if you are asking me to sacrifice what is genuinely good in me so that you can gain what is not good, see how unfair you are. Which would you rather have — money, or a friend who is faithful and honorable? Help me to be that kind of friend, then, and don't ask me to become someone who would no longer be one. "But you will be no use to your country!" Again — what use? It won't owe you its colonnades or its public baths. But the smith doesn't provide shoes and the cobbler doesn't provide weapons — it is enough that every person does their own work. If you gave the country one more honest and honorable citizen, would you not be useful to it? Yes. Then you can be useful to it. What role will you play? Whatever you can, while maintaining your honesty and honor. But if by trying to be useful you lose those qualities, what good are you to anyone once you have become dishonest and unprincipled?

chapters.title: Section 25
paragraphs: Was someone else given a higher place at a banquet, or greeted more warmly, or consulted first? If these things are good, be glad they got them; if bad, don't be troubled that you didn't. And remember: if you don't do what others do to obtain things outside your power, you cannot claim an equal share. How can you expect to be treated like someone who flatters and attends and praises the host, when you yourself do none of that? It would be unfair and unreasonable to want the goods without paying the price. What is the price of a head of lettuce? One coin, perhaps. If someone pays the coin, they get the lettuce. If you don't pay, you don't get it. But don't think you've come away with less than the person who has the lettuce — you still have the coin you didn't pay. In the same way, you weren't invited to someone's dinner: you didn't pay the price the host charges, which is flattery and personal attention. If you think it's worth paying, then pay it. But if you want both — to keep your self-respect and to have the dinner — you are being greedy and foolish. What do you have instead of the dinner? You have the fact of not having flattered the person you chose not to flatter. You have not having to endure their company.

chapters.title: Section 26
paragraphs: We can learn what nature wants from the things on which we all agree. When your neighbour's slave breaks a cup, you say straightaway: "These things happen." You must know that when your own cup breaks, you should think the same. Apply this to larger things too. When someone else's child or wife dies, anyone would say: "That is the human condition." But when your own child or wife dies, you cry out: "What a disaster, how wretched I am!" Remember how you felt when you heard it happen to someone else.

chapters.title: Section 27
paragraphs: A target is not set up in order to be missed. In the same way, evil does not naturally exist in the world.

chapters.title: Section 28
paragraphs: If someone threatened to hand your body over to the first person you met on the road, you would be outraged. And yet you hand your mind over to whoever happens to cross your path — so that if they insult you, it is thrown into confusion and turmoil. Are you not ashamed?

chapters.title: Section 29
paragraphs: Before taking on any action, consider what comes first and what follows from it. Then proceed. If you don't, you will begin with enthusiasm, not having thought through the consequences, and then feel ashamed when difficulties appear. A man wants to win at the Olympic games. Fine — so would I, it's a wonderful thing. But first consider what comes before and what follows after. You must live by strict routine, eat under orders, avoid sweets, train at set times in heat and cold, drink no cold water, drink no wine except as prescribed — in short, surrender yourself to the trainer as you would to a doctor. Then in the contest itself, you may sprain a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a mouthful of sand, be flogged — and after all that, be beaten. Consider all this first. If you still want to go ahead, then go. Otherwise you will behave like a child who plays at being a wrestler one minute, a gladiator the next, then a trumpeter, then an actor — you too will be an athlete today, a philosopher tomorrow, an orator the day after, nothing with your whole soul. Like a monkey, you imitate whatever you see, and each new thing catches your fancy before you have considered whether it suits you. Someone sees a philosopher and hears him speak well, and immediately wants to become a philosopher too. My friend, first consider what kind of thing philosophy is. Then examine your own nature to see whether you are capable of bearing it. Do you want to be a wrestler? Look at your arms, your thighs. Different people are made for different things. Do you think you can pursue philosophy and still eat and drink and want and avoid the same things as before? You will have to stay up at night, endure hardship, leave your family, be looked down on by a servant, be last in everything — in status, in honor, in the courts. Consider whether you are willing to trade all this for freedom from passion, for liberty, for tranquility. If not, don't become a philosopher — don't be like the child who is a philosopher today and a tax collector tomorrow. Choose one thing. You are either a good person or not. Either you cultivate your own mind or you chase external things. There is no combining them.

chapters.title: Section 30
paragraphs: Duties are always grounded in relationships. Is someone your father? You are meant to care for him, yield to him in all things, endure his criticism and even his harshness. But what if he is a bad father? You were not made to be related to a good father — only to a father. Is your brother wronging you? Keep to your own position toward him, and don't ask what he is doing but what you must do so that your will stays aligned with nature. No one can damage you unless you allow it — you are only damaged when you decide you have been damaged. This is how you discover your duty from any relationship: neighbour, citizen, commander — once you get into the habit of seeing relationships clearly.

chapters.title: Section 31
paragraphs: Regarding piety toward the gods: the most important thing is to have right opinions about them — to believe they exist and that they govern everything well and justly. Fix yourself in this: to obey them, to yield to them in whatever happens, and to follow events willingly, knowing they proceed from the highest wisdom. If you do this, you will never blame the gods or accuse them of neglecting you. This is only possible if you stop treating things outside your control as good or bad. If you think anything outside your control is good or bad, then whenever you fail to get what you want or fall into what you don't want, you will find fault and hate whoever seems to be the cause. Every creature by nature flees what seems harmful and pursues what seems useful — so it is impossible to be glad about something you think is harming you, just as it is impossible to be glad about harm itself. This is why a son curses his father when the father withholds what the son considers good; why Polynices and Eteocles became enemies — each thinking the kingship was the good. This is why farmers, sailors, and merchants curse the gods, and why people curse them when they lose their wives and children. Where your interest lies, so does your piety. So whoever takes care to desire and avoid rightly also takes care in piety along the way. But make offerings and sacrifices and first fruits in keeping with the customs of your ancestors — purely, not meanly, not carelessly, not below your means, not beyond them. This is everyone's obligation.

chapters.title: Section 32
paragraphs: When you consult a diviner, remember that you don't know what the outcome will be — that is why you are consulting. But you do know, if you are a philosopher, that the outcome will be one of the things outside your control, and therefore neither good nor bad in itself. Don't bring desire or aversion to the diviner — if you do, you will arrive in fear. Instead, having settled in your mind that every possible outcome is morally neutral and beyond your power to change, though never beyond your power to use well, come confidently to the gods as your advisers. When advice is given, remember who you have taken as your advisers, and whose guidance you will have ignored if you don't follow it. Go to divination, as Socrates said, only about things where the outcome cannot be determined by reason or skill. So when the situation calls for you to share in a friend's or your country's danger, don't go and ask the diviner whether you should. Even if the diviner tells you the omens are bad — that death or injury or exile is threatened — reason already tells you that you should share the danger. The greater diviner is the god at Delphi, who drove from the temple the man who failed to stand by his friend when his friend was being murdered.

chapters.title: Section 33
paragraphs: Set yourself a character and a standard right now, and keep to it both when you are alone and when you are in company.

As a rule, be silent — or say only what needs to be said, in few words. Rarely, and when the occasion calls for it, speak — but not about the usual subjects: not about gladiators, horse races, athletes, food or drink, and above all not about other people — not to criticise them, praise them, or compare them. If you can, bring your companions' conversation toward something worthwhile. If you find yourself among strangers, stay silent.
Don't laugh much, or often, or loudly.
Avoid taking oaths altogether if you can. If you cannot avoid it, avoid it as much as possible.

Avoid banquets given by outsiders and the uninstructed. If you do have occasion to attend, be on your guard not to fall into common habits. Know that if your companion is impure, even a pure person who keeps their company becomes impure.
Take care of your body only as far as basic needs: food, drink, clothing, a house, servants. Cut out everything that is for show or luxury.

As for sexual pleasure, abstain as much as you can before marriage. If you do indulge, do so within accepted norms. But don't be disapproving or preachy to those who do indulge, and don't make a point of announcing how well you have avoided it.
If someone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, don't defend yourself against what was reported. Simply say: "He must not know my other faults, or he would have mentioned those too."

You don't need to go to the theatre often. If you do go on occasion, don't show yourself as a partisan of any performer — want only what happens to happen, and let the winner win. That way you will meet no frustration. But hold back entirely from shouting, being swept up in emotion, or laughing loudly at anything. When you leave, don't talk much about what you saw on stage, except about things that might improve you. If you talk a great deal about the performance, it is plain you were more affected than you should have been.
Don't readily attend public readings or lectures. But if you do attend, maintain composure and seriousness, and avoid making yourself disagreeable.

When you are about to meet someone — especially someone considered powerful or important — think to yourself: what would Socrates or Zeno have done here? You will have no difficulty knowing how to conduct yourself.

When visiting someone in power, tell yourself in advance: you may not be admitted; the door may not open; the person may not care about you. If it is still right to go, then go, and accept whatever happens. Don't say afterward that it wasn't worth the trouble. That is the response of someone governed by externals.

In company, don't talk at length about your own exploits or dangers. It may be pleasant for you to recall them, but it is not pleasant for others to hear. And be careful not to provoke laughter — this is a path toward vulgar habits and tends to diminish the respect of those around you. Obscene talk is a dangerous drift. If it arises and there is a good opening, rebuke the person who started it. If there is no good opening, at the very least show by your silence, your expression, and your manner that you find it distasteful.

chapters.title: Section 34
paragraphs: When a pleasure presents itself, be on your guard against being swept away. Give it some time — allow yourself a pause. Then think of both moments: the moment of the pleasure and the moment after, when you will feel regret and reproach yourself. Then weigh against those the satisfaction you will feel if you resist, and the pride you will take in yourself. But if you do decide the time is right, be careful that the pleasure's charm and attraction don't overwhelm you — put on the other side how much better it is to know you won this one.

chapters.title: Section 35
paragraphs: When you have decided that something is right to do, do it openly without concern for what people think. If it is the wrong thing to do, don't do it. If it is right, why fear the criticism of those who are wrong about it?

chapters.title: Section 36
paragraphs: In logic, "it is either day or it is night" is very useful in a disjunctive argument but useless in a conjunctive one. In the same way, at a dinner, taking the larger share is good for your body but terrible for maintaining the spirit of the occasion. When you eat with others, remember not only the value of the food to your body, but also the value of treating your host well.

chapters.title: Section 37
paragraphs: If you have taken on a role beyond your strength, you have failed in two ways: you have not performed it, and you have left undone what you might have managed well.

chapters.title: Section 38
paragraphs: Just as in walking you watch out for a nail in the ground or a twisted ankle, watch out equally for anything that damages your own ruling mind. If we observe this in every action, we will go about each task more safely.

chapters.title: Section 39
paragraphs: The body is the measure of what you need, just as the foot is the measure of the shoe. If you keep to this standard, you keep your measure. Once you go beyond it, you go off a cliff: first the shoe is gilded, then dyed purple, then embroidered. Once you have passed the true measure, there is no limit.

chapters.title: Section 40
paragraphs: Girls from the age of fourteen are called "mistresses" by men. And so, seeing that they have nothing else to offer, they begin to make themselves attractive and place all their hopes in their appearance. It is worth taking care, therefore, that they understand they are valued for nothing but being decent, modest, and self-possessed.

chapters.title: Section 41
paragraphs: It is a sign of a low mind to devote excessive time to the body's needs — too much exercise, too much eating, too much drinking, too much indulgence. These things belong in the category of secondary concerns. Let your real care be directed toward the mind.

chapters.title: Section 42
paragraphs: When someone treats you badly or speaks ill of you, remember that they do so because it seems right to them. They cannot follow what seems right to you — only what seems right to them. If they are wrong, they are the one who is harmed, for they are the one who has been deceived. When you understand this, you will be gentle toward those who speak against you. In each case say to yourself: it seemed right to them.

chapters.title: Section 43
paragraphs: Everything has two handles — one by which it can be carried, one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of it by the handle of the wrong — that is the handle that cannot be borne. Take hold of it by the other handle: that he is your brother, that you grew up together. Taken by that handle, it can be carried.

chapters.title: Section 44
paragraphs: These arguments don't follow: "I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you"; "I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better than you." But these do follow: "I am richer than you, therefore my wealth is greater than yours"; "I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speaking is better than yours." But you are neither your wealth nor your speaking.

chapters.title: Section 45
paragraphs: Does someone bathe quickly? Don't say they bathe badly — say they bathe quickly. Does someone drink a lot of wine? Don't say they do it badly — say they drink a lot. Without knowing what they are thinking, how can you say whether they are doing wrong? Don't rush to assent to impressions before you have tested them.

chapters.title: Section 46
paragraphs: Never call yourself a philosopher, and don't talk at length to uninstructed people about philosophical arguments. Show what you have learned through action. At a dinner party, don't lecture people about how one ought to eat — eat as one ought. Remember how completely Socrates avoided showing off. People would come to him and ask to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them along — so readily did he keep himself in the background. If a philosophical topic comes up among uninstructed people, generally stay silent — it is very easy to start talking before you have properly digested what you know. When someone tells you that you know nothing and you are not stung by it, that is when you know you have actually begun philosophy. Even sheep don't regurgitate their grass to show the shepherd how much they have eaten — they digest it and produce wool and milk. Don't display your principles to the uninstructed. Display the conduct that comes from digesting them.

chapters.title: Section 47
paragraphs: When your bodily needs are met simply and cheaply, don't make a point of it. If you drink water, don't announce it constantly. Consider first how much more frugal the genuinely poor are than we, and how much more they endure. If you want to train yourself in hardship, do it for yourself, not for others. Don't embrace statues in the cold. If you are very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.

chapters.title: Section 48
paragraphs: The condition of an uninstructed person is this: they expect all their benefit and all their harm to come from externals. The condition of a philosopher is this: they expect all benefit and all harm from themselves. The signs of someone making progress: they blame no one, they praise no one, they complain about no one, they accuse no one, they say nothing about themselves as if they were important or knew something. When they are hindered or frustrated, they blame themselves. If someone praises them, they laugh at the praise to themselves. If someone censures them, they make no defence. They move carefully, like a convalescent, so as not to disturb anything before it has properly healed. They have cleared out all desire. They have redirected aversion to only those things within their control that are genuinely contrary to nature. Their impulses are moderate throughout. Whether they seem foolish or ignorant, they don't care. In a word, they watch themselves as if they were an enemy lying in wait.

chapters.title: Section 49
paragraphs: When someone is proud of being able to explain the writings of Chrysippus, say to yourself: if Chrysippus had written more clearly, this person would have nothing to be proud of. What do I want? To understand nature and follow it. So I look for a guide. When I hear it is Chrysippus, I go to him. But I don't understand what he wrote, so I look for an interpreter. So far, there is nothing to be proud of. When I find the interpreter, what remains is to use what I have learned — that is the only thing to be proud of. If instead I just admire the explanation, I have become a literary critic, not a philosopher — except that I am analysing Chrysippus instead of Homer. When someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I feel ashamed when I cannot point to conduct that matches what I have read.

chapters.title: Section 50
paragraphs: Whatever principles you have decided on for your conduct, hold to them as if they were laws — as if you would be breaking a sacred duty to violate them. Whatever anyone says about you, do not be concerned with it. This is none of your business. How long will you keep putting off the decision to be worthy of the best things, and to obey the reason that distinguishes you in every particular? You have accepted the principles you were meant to accept. What further teacher are you waiting for? You are no longer a boy. You are a grown person. If you go on being negligent and lazy, always postponing, making plan after plan, setting day after day after which you will finally pay attention to yourself — you will die without having improved, and you will never even know it. Start now: decide to live as an adult, as someone making real progress. Let what you truly believe to be best be a law you never break. If something hard or pleasant or glorious or inglorious is placed before you, the contest is now. The Olympic games are not deferred. A single defeat, a single surrender, and the progress already made is either lost or secured. This is how Socrates became what he was — improving in everything, attending to nothing but reason. Even if you are not yet Socrates, you ought to live like someone who wants to be.

chapters.title: Section 51
paragraphs: The first and most necessary part of philosophy is putting principles into practice — for instance: you must not lie. The second part is providing demonstrations: how do we know you must not lie? The third part is securing and explaining those demonstrations: what is a demonstration? What is entailment? What is contradiction? What is truth, what is falsehood? The third part is needed to support the second, and the second to support the first. But the first is the most important — the one we should rest in. We do the opposite. We spend all our time on the third part, applying all our enthusiasm to it, while entirely neglecting the first. So we lie — but we have the demonstration that we ought not to lie readily to hand.

chapters.title: Section 52
paragraphs: In every situation, keep these three maxims ready:
Lead me, Zeus, and you too, Destiny — wherever you have appointed me to go. I will follow without hesitation. And if I refuse and prove base, I shall follow nonetheless.
Whoever yields to necessity with grace, we call wise, and one who understands the divine.
And this third also: Crito, if it pleases the gods, so let it be. Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot harm me.
